context.concept_name: Date functions and date arithmetic (TODAY, DATEDIF)

coverage.learning_objective: Compute a date-based value, such as an age in years, using TODAY together with DATEDIF.

required_facts.statement: The TODAY function returns the serial number of the current date and takes no arguments; its syntax is TODAY().

The DATEDIF function returns the difference between a start_date and an end_date in the unit you specify; its syntax is DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit), where a unit of "Y" returns the number of complete years in the period.
DATEDIF is useful in formulas where you need to calculate an age.
Excel stores dates as sequential serial numbers so they can be used in calculations; by default, January 1, 1900 is serial number 1.
DATEDIF's unit argument "D" returns the number of days in the period between start_date and end_date.

teaching_blocks.content: Excel stores dates as sequential serial numbers so they can be used in calculations; by default, January 1, 1900 is serial number 1. That's why date functions can do arithmetic on dates the same way ordinary functions do on numbers.
The TODAY function returns the serial number of the current date and takes no arguments; its syntax is TODAY().

The DATEDIF function returns the difference between a start_date and an end_date in the unit you specify; its syntax is DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit), where a unit of "Y" returns the number of complete years in the period, and a unit of "D" returns the number of days in the period. DATEDIF is useful in formulas where you need to calculate an age.
On your Orders sheet, with an order date in G2, =DATEDIF(G2,TODAY(),"D") would tell you how many days have passed since that order was placed.

coverage.learning_objective: Aggregate only the rows that match one or more conditions using COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, SUMIF, or SUMIFS.

required_facts.statement: COUNTIF counts the number of cells in a range that meet a single criterion; its syntax is COUNTIF(range, criteria).

COUNTIFS applies criteria to cells across multiple ranges and counts the number of times all the criteria are met together; its syntax is COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...), and each additional range must have the same number of rows and columns as criteria_range1.

SUMIF sums the values in a range that meet criteria you specify, optionally applying the criteria to one range while summing the corresponding values in a different range; its syntax is SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]).

SUMIFS adds the cells in a sum_range that meet multiple criteria at once, where each criteria_range/criteria pair is a separate condition that must all be met; its syntax is SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...).

Criteria for these functions can be a number, expression, cell reference, or text, such as 32, ">32", B4, or "apples"; criteria containing comparison symbols or text must be enclosed in quotation marks.
The same range can be used in more than one criteria pair to test a range condition, for example =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<6",A2:A7,">1") counts values between 1 and 6.

teaching_blocks.content: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT and COUNTA all take every value in the range you give them. Often you only want the rows that meet some condition -- orders from one city, say.

COUNTIF counts the number of cells in a range that meet a single criterion; its syntax is COUNTIF(range, criteria). SUMIF sums the values in a range that meet criteria you specify, optionally applying the criteria to one range while summing the corresponding values in a different range; its syntax is SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]). =COUNTIF(B2:B51,"Lagos") counts Lagos orders; =SUMIF(B2:B51,"Lagos",D2:D51) sums their amounts.

COUNTIFS applies criteria to cells across multiple ranges and counts the number of times all the criteria are met together; its syntax is COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...), and each additional range must have the same number of rows and columns as criteria_range1. SUMIFS adds the cells in a sum_range that meet multiple criteria at once, where each criteria_range/criteria pair is a separate condition that must all be met; its syntax is SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...). =SUMIFS(D2:D51,B2:B51,"Lagos",E2:E51,"Delivered") sums only the Lagos orders that are also marked Delivered.

Criteria for these functions can be a number, expression, cell reference, or text, such as 32, ">32", B4, or "apples"; criteria containing comparison symbols or text must be enclosed in quotation marks. The same range can be used in more than one criteria pair to test a range condition, for example =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<6",A2:A7,">1") counts values between 1 and 6 -- the same trick would let you count deliveries with a delivery time between 10 and 60 minutes using =COUNTIFS(C2:C51,">10",C2:C51,"<60").

video_need.reason: Lining up which criteria_range pairs with which criteria across a multi-condition COUNTIFS or SUMIFS is easy to get backwards from reading syntax alone -- watching one built live, argument by argument, against a real range makes the pairing concrete.

media.group_title: Building conditional aggregation formulas argument by argument

segments.label: SUMIF and SUMIFS: summing revenue for one condition, then two, then three
segments.summary: A dataset of months, products, countries, and sales revenue is used to build SUMIF for a single criterion (February revenue): the criteria range comes first, then the criterion, then the sum range at the end. SUMIFS is then built for two criteria (February and shirt white), with the sum range moved to the front and criteria_range1/criteria1/criteria_range2/criteria2 following in pairs. A third criterion (USA) is added by appending one more range–criteria pair, and each result is verified against the visible data.

segments.label: COUNTIF and COUNTIFS: counting rows that match one or two conditions
segments.summary: A spreadsheet table of builders and regions is used to build COUNTIF step by step: the criteria range is selected first, then the criterion is entered as a quoted text string, then as a cell reference copied down the column. The formula correctly returns one instance of Doug, two of Dave, two of Brian, and one of Larry. COUNTIFS is then introduced to add a second condition — builder name paired with region — showing how criteria_range1/criteria1 and criteria_range2/criteria2 are entered in sequence; the result correctly returns zero for Doug (who is in the Central region), one for Brian, and one for Larry in the South.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each argument slot is filled in order. The first clip uses text criteria only; the second clip uses both text and cell-reference criteria — no comparison operators like ">32" appear in either.
bridge_note.after: The clips do not show criteria with comparison operators, the quoting rule for expressions, or the same-range-twice trick for between-value counts — the teaching text covers all three.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a sales table with columns Region, Date, and Amount, write a SUMIFS formula that totals Amount only for rows where Region equals a specified value and Date falls within a given date range, using three criteria_range/criteria pairs (one for Region, two for the Date range boundaries).
practice_anchor.success: The formula returns the correct total that matches a manual filter of the table for the specified region and date range, with no #VALUE! or #NAME? errors.

coverage.learning_objective: Write a VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP formula that finds a key in a table and returns a corresponding value from another column.

required_facts.statement: VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position; its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]).

In VLOOKUP, entering FALSE (or 0) for range_lookup searches for an exact match to lookup_value; leaving range_lookup blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match instead, and TRUE is the default if the argument is omitted.

HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position; its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default; its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]).
VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction and returns exact matches by default.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose your Drivers sheet has driver IDs in its leftmost column and driver names in the column next to it, and your Orders sheet records a driver ID in column F. You want each order row to show the matching driver's name.

VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position; its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]). In VLOOKUP, entering FALSE (or 0) for range_lookup searches for an exact match to lookup_value; leaving range_lookup blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match instead, and TRUE is the default if the argument is omitted. Looking up a driver ID with =VLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:B,2,FALSE) searches for an exact match to the driver ID in F2; leaving the last argument off would search for an approximate match instead.

HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position; its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default; its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction. The same driver lookup written as =XLOOKUP(F2,Drivers!A:A,Drivers!B:B) already matches exactly, without needing FALSE spelled out.

video_need.reason: Watching a lookup formula scan down a key column and pull back a value from another column -- and watching an exact match go wrong when range_lookup is left as an approximate match by default -- is a mechanism that's far easier to follow demonstrated than described.

media.group_title: Lookup functions in action: VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP

segments.label: Building a VLOOKUP formula: key column, return column, and exact-match argument
segments.summary: A VLOOKUP formula is assembled argument by argument against a sales dataset. The lookup value is a name; the table range covers the salesperson column through the sales column; the column index is set to 3 because the target data sits in the third column of that range. The final argument is explained as the match-type switch: FALSE forces an exact match, which is the right choice in almost all business cases. TRUE, or omitting the argument entirely, triggers approximate matching and should only be used when the data is already sorted — and even then the results may be unreliable. The formula is then made dynamic by pointing the lookup value to a cell so that changing the cell updates the result.

segments.label: Building an XLOOKUP formula: lookup array, return array, and the if_not_found argument
segments.summary: XLOOKUP is introduced as a finding tool: given a name in a cell, it locates that name in a lookup column and returns the corresponding value from a separate return column. The formula is built in argument order — lookup value (pointed to a cell or typed directly), lookup array (the name column, B8:B42), return array (the job-title column, G8:G42) — and returns the correct result immediately. Pointing to a cell rather than hard-coding a value makes the formula reusable. When the lookup value is absent from the data, XLOOKUP returns an #N/A error; the fourth argument, if_not_found, lets you supply a custom message such as 'no such person' instead.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each argument is chosen and what the match-type argument does in the first clip; in the second, note the separate lookup array and return array — XLOOKUP's key structural difference from VLOOKUP.
bridge_note.after: Neither clip covers HLOOKUP or XLOOKUP's direction advantage over VLOOKUP; the teaching text fills both gaps. Error values (#N/A) shown in the second clip are a later topic — ignore them here.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a two-column price table with product IDs in the left column and prices in the right column, write an XLOOKUP formula in a separate cell that retrieves the price for a given product ID.
practice_anchor.success: The formula uses XLOOKUP with the product ID cell as lookup_value, the product-ID column as lookup_array, and the price column as return_array, and returns the correct price when the product ID exists in the table.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a two-sheet layout: a Drivers (or Products) reference table with IDs in the leftmost column and a second column of values, alongside an Orders (or Transactions) sheet where the lookup formula sits — making the left-to-right constraint of VLOOKUP and the separate-array structure of XLOOKUP immediately visible.

coverage.learning_objective: Combine INDEX and MATCH to look up a value when the return column is not to the right of the key column.

required_facts.statement: MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range; its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]).

Setting MATCH's match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value that is less than or equal to lookup_value, and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position; the array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, meaning the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value; when the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

teaching_blocks.content: VLOOKUP only works when the column you're returning a value from sits to the right of the key column. If your Drivers sheet instead had driver names in column A and driver IDs in column B, VLOOKUP couldn't look up an ID and return the name to its left.

MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range; its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]). Setting MATCH's match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value that is less than or equal to lookup_value, and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position; the array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, meaning the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value; when the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position. So on your Orders sheet, with an order's driver ID in F2, =INDEX(Drivers!A:A,MATCH(F2,Drivers!B:B,0)) finds the row where that driver ID occurs in the Drivers sheet's column B, then reads the driver name from column A at that same row -- something VLOOKUP alone couldn't do on this layout.

video_need.reason: Seeing MATCH return a row position and then watching INDEX use that same position to pull a value from a completely different column makes the two-step handoff between the functions concrete in a way that reading the nested formula doesn't.

media.group_title: INDEX and MATCH working together: a two-step lookup

segments.label: Live demo: INDEX/MATCH formula with an exact-match lookup
segments.summary: A spreadsheet holds employee names in one column and join dates in another; the goal is to return the name for a given date. The presenter builds =INDEX(name column, MATCH(input date, date column, 0)), explaining that MATCH first finds the row position of the date and INDEX then returns the name at that position. The formula is then split into its two parts to show each step: MATCH alone returns 6 (the sixth date), and INDEX alone on the names list returns the sixth name, confirming how the two functions hand off to each other.

bridge_note.before: Watch how MATCH produces a row number and INDEX consumes it. The return column (names) sits left of the lookup column (dates) — the exact layout VLOOKUP cannot handle.
bridge_note.after: The clip shows only exact-match (match_type 0) and does not cover match_type 1 or the sorting requirement; the teaching text covers both.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a two-column reference sheet where names appear in column A and IDs appear in column B, write an INDEX/MATCH formula on a separate sheet that looks up an ID from column B and returns the corresponding name from column A.
practice_anchor.success: The formula uses INDEX on the names column and MATCH with match_type 0 on the IDs column, returns the correct name for the given ID, and does not use VLOOKUP.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a two-column reference table with the return value (e.g. driver name) in column A and the lookup key (e.g. driver ID) in column B, making the left-of-key layout concrete and illustrating why VLOOKUP cannot be used here.

context.concept_name: Common formula error values and troubleshooting (#N/A, #REF!, #VALUE!)

coverage.learning_objective: Given a formula's error value, diagnose which class of problem — a failed lookup, an invalid reference, or a wrong data type — is causing it.

required_facts.statement: The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for; the most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data.
The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over.
#VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing.

A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return a #VALUE! error if any of the referenced cells contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error.

teaching_blocks.content: Formulas in your Orders or Drivers sheets sometimes show an error code instead of a value. Each code points at a different kind of problem.

The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for; the most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data. A VLOOKUP for a driver ID that was never entered on the Drivers sheet would show #N/A.

The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over. Deleting the amount column that a SUM formula depended on would turn that formula into a #REF! error.

#VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing. A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return a #VALUE! error if any of the referenced cells contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones -- so typing a stray note into an amount cell breaks a plain + formula but not a SUM over the same range.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error too -- so one bad cell's error can spread into a SUM or AVERAGE built on top of it.

video_need.reason: Recognizing which error code you're looking at, and seeing how a bad cell's #VALUE! error propagates into a SUM or AVERAGE built over it, is easier to spot when watched happening on a real sheet than described in the abstract.

media.group_title: Seeing formula errors appear and propagate on a live sheet

segments.label: How #VALUE!, #REF!, and #N/A errors appear in a real spreadsheet
segments.summary: The presenter works through several error codes on a live sheet. For #VALUE!, a subtraction formula breaks the moment a cell holds the text 'missing'; wrapping the same calculation inside SUM makes the error disappear because SUM skips text values. For #REF!, deleting a column that a formula depended on immediately turns that formula into a #REF! error; copying and pasting the formula to a location where its relative reference points off the grid does the same. Two additional errors (#SPILL! and #NAME?) are shown briefly: #SPILL! appears when a spilling function is blocked by a non-empty cell, and #NAME? appears when a function name is mistyped. For #DIV/0!, dividing by an empty cell (treated as zero) triggers the error, and IFERROR is used to suppress it. Finally, #N/A is demonstrated with a VLOOKUP that cannot find 'Limbo' because the correct spelling in the source data is 'Limba'; IFNA is then used to return a custom message instead of the error code.

bridge_note.before: Watch how a single text cell breaks a subtraction formula but not SUM, and how deleting a column instantly produces #REF!. Note: the clip also shows #SPILL!, #NAME?, and #DIV/0! — those are outside this lesson.
bridge_note.after: The clip does not show a #VALUE! error spreading from one cell into a SUM or AVERAGE built on top of it (f5); the teaching text covers that propagation behaviour.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a worksheet containing a broken VLOOKUP showing #N/A (because the lookup value is misspelled relative to the source data) and a broken addition formula showing #VALUE! (because one cell in the range holds a text value), identify the cause of each error and state which change would resolve each one.
practice_anchor.success: The learner correctly names the cause of the #N/A error (lookup value not found in source data) and the cause of the #VALUE! error (a text value in a cell referenced by an arithmetic formula), and correctly states that replacing the misspelled lookup value would fix the #N/A and that switching the addition formula to SUM would resolve the #VALUE! without removing the text cell.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a small Orders-style sheet with three visible error states side by side: a VLOOKUP returning #N/A, an arithmetic formula returning #VALUE! next to a SUM over the same range returning a number, and a formula returning #REF! after its referenced column has been deleted — so learners can match each error code to its visual context.

context.concept_name: Pivot tables: rows, columns, values, filters

coverage.learning_objective: Build a PivotTable that places one field in Rows, another in Columns, and a numeric field in Values.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable to analyze worksheet data

required_facts.statement: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable in Excel for Windows

required_facts.statement: To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

teaching_blocks.content: Reading down a long Orders sheet to compare total amounts by city and status by hand would take forever. A PivotTable does that comparison for you.
A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.

To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK. To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable. Building a PivotTable from your Orders data with City dragged into Rows, Status dragged into Columns, and Amount left in Values gives a grid of summarized order amounts for every city/status combination at once.

video_need.reason: Dragging fields between the Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters areas and watching the summary grid rearrange itself is exactly the kind of changing-state, tool-usage demonstration that's much faster to show than to narrate field by field.

media.group_title: Building a PivotTable: fields, areas, and layout

segments.label: Create a PivotTable and place fields in Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters

On the right-hand side, four drop zones appear: Filters, Columns, Rows, and Values. Salesperson is dragged to Rows and Amount to Values, producing a total-sales-per-salesperson summary. A third PivotTable places Geography in Filters, which adds a top-level filter control above the table so results can be narrowed to a single geography such as New Zealand.

bridge_note.after: The clip shows all four areas in action. Note that the checkbox default-placement rule (non-numeric → Rows, numeric → Values) is stated in the text but not narrated in the clip.

practice_anchor.success: The completed PivotTable has Region in the Rows area, Product Category in the Columns area, and Sales Amount in the Values area, producing a grid of totals for every Region/Product Category combination.

context.concept_name: Pivot table summarization options (sum, count, average)

coverage.learning_objective: Change a PivotTable value field's summary function, recognizing that Sum is the default for numeric fields.

required_facts.statement: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarizes the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_summary_guide#Change the summary function or custom calculation for a field in a PivotTable

required_facts.statement: To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the summary function you want, such as Average.

teaching_blocks.content: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarizes the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values. Placing Amount in Values on your Orders PivotTable defaults to a total of every matching order's amount, not an average.

To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the summary function you want, such as Average. Switching Amount from Sum to Average turns the same PivotTable from showing total revenue per city into showing average order value per city, without changing which fields are in Rows or Columns.

video_need.reason: Watching the numbers in an existing PivotTable recompute the instant the summary setting is switched from Sum to Average is a clear before/after that a quick demo shows in seconds.

media.group_title: Changing a PivotTable's value-field summary function

segments.label: Opening Value Field Settings to switch a summary function from Sum to Average
segments.summary: Starting from a PivotTable that already has a numeric field in the Values area, the presenter opens Value Field Settings two ways: first by clicking the field's dropdown arrow in the Values area and selecting Value Field Settings, then by right-clicking the value cell in the PivotTable itself. In both cases the same dialog appears; selecting Average and clicking OK immediately updates the displayed numbers, and the process is reversed by returning to the dialog and selecting Sum.

segments.label: Why a PivotTable value field defaults to Count for text and Sum for numbers
segments.summary: A PivotTable's Values area automatically chooses its calculation type based on the data type of the field: text fields default to Count because text cannot be summed, while numeric fields default to Sum. A numeric column that contains blank cells is treated as mixed and also defaults to Count; the same applies to columns containing error values such as #REF! or #N/A.

bridge_note.before: The first clip shows both routes into Value Field Settings to switch to Average (f2); the second explains the Count-vs-Sum default rule (f1). Watch for the two entry points: the dropdown and the right-click menu.
bridge_note.after: Neither clip covers the full step-by-step path on the PivotTable Analyze tab (Active Field > Field Settings); the teaching text fills that gap and remains the complete reference.

practice_anchor.objective: Open an existing PivotTable that shows total order amounts per city (Sum), navigate to Value Field Settings, switch the summary function to Average, and explain in one sentence how the displayed numbers changed and what they now represent.
practice_anchor.success: The Values area header updates to 'Average of Amount', each city row shows a per-order average rather than a total, and the learner's written sentence correctly contrasts total revenue with average order value.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the same PivotTable side-by-side: left panel with Sum of Amount per city, right panel with Average of Amount per city, so the learner can see how the same row/column structure produces different numbers depending on the summary function.

coverage.learning_objective: Build a bar chart from a summary table, arranging category and value data in columns or rows before inserting the chart.

required_facts.statement: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organized along one axis and the values along the other.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

teaching_blocks.content: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organized along one axis and the values along the other. A summary table of total order amount by city is exactly the kind of category-versus-value data a bar chart compares.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.

video_need.reason: A bar chart's whole point is visual comparison, so seeing the finished chart -- and the Recommended Charts preview step that produces it -- is worth showing, even though the two-step creation process is simple enough to follow from text.

media.group_title: Building a bar chart in Excel: selecting data and reading the result

segments.label: Selecting data and inserting a column/bar chart from the Charts group
segments.summary: The presenter highlights a monthly sales table, opens the Insert tab, and picks a 2-D column chart directly from the Charts gallery. After inserting, they explore chart style options and the Switch Row/Column toggle to flip which dimension appears on each axis. They then use the chart's filter to remove a totals row and a year-end total column that were distorting the scale, apply the change, and add a title. The finished chart shows months along the horizontal axis and bar heights representing product quantities, making it easy to see that paper is the top-selling product every month.

segments.label: Insert > Column Chart button: selecting data and fixing category order
segments.summary: Starting from a selected data range, the presenter goes to the Insert tab, clicks the Column Chart button, and chooses the bar chart option. context.concept_name: matplotlib figure and axes object model

coverage.learning_objective: Recognize matplotlib's Figure/Axes object model: identify which calls create the Figure vs. the Axes, and create a Figure with one Axes to plot on.

required_facts.statement: Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.
fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects.
Plotting calls such as ax.plot(x, y) draw onto that specific Axes object.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you have this week's delivery times -- 18, 22, 26, 19, 30 minutes -- and you want to see them as a graph instead of a list of numbers. Matplotlib is the library that draws that graph, but it draws onto two different kinds of object, not just "a plot". Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.

The Figure is the overall canvas: the whole window or image you eventually display or save. An Axes is one plotting area that lives inside that Figure -- the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where lines, bars, or points are actually drawn. A single Figure can hold more than one Axes, but even the simplest plot needs at least one.

After `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`, `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects: `fig` refers to the whole canvas, and `ax` refers to the one plotting area inside it.

Plotting calls such as `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto that specific Axes object. `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` followed by `ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` draws the week's delivery times as a line onto `ax`. `fig` itself doesn't receive any plotted data directly -- it just holds the Axes that does.

With `plt.subplots()`, you get a Figure and an Axes first, then call a plotting method on the Axes, not the Figure. Keeping the two straight -- Figure is the canvas, Axes is where the data goes -- makes plotting calls like `ax.plot()` easier to read.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a basic plot from data using matplotlib's pyplot interface, with the correct plt.plot() argument form.

required_facts.statement: plt.plot(y) called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0.

teaching_blocks.content: You have already seen `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto an Axes you created with `plt.subplots()`. pyplot also has its own `plot()` function, called directly as `plt.plot()`, and it accepts data in two different forms.

`plt.plot(y)` called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0. Given just the delivery times `[18, 22, 26, 19, 30]`, `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots those five values against the automatic x-positions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

`plt.plot(x, y)` called with two array arguments plots the y-values against the given x-values instead. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots the same five delivery times, but now against the day numbers 1 through 5 you supplied, rather than the automatic 0-based positions.
Both forms call the same function and produce a similar-looking line; the only difference is whether you hand `plot()` an explicit x-axis or let it fill one in for you starting at 0.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a bar chart with matplotlib to compare a numeric value across discrete categories, aligning bars to a common baseline.

required_facts.statement: plt.bar(x, height) (or ax.bar(x, height)) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0.
A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups.
Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline.
Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument to plt.bar() (for example plt.bar(names, values)), rather than only numeric x-positions.

misconceptions.statement: A bar's baseline can start at any value without distorting the comparison.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare average delivery time across three cities -- Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- rather than look at individual deliveries. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups, which fits this comparison exactly.

`plt.bar(x, height)` (or `ax.bar(x, height)`) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0. Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument, rather than only numeric x-positions: `city_avg = orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` stores one average per city, with the city names as its index, and `plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg)` plots those three city names directly as the bars' x-positions, with each city's average as its bar height.

Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline -- here, every bar starts at 0, so the bar for Kano simply looks taller than Lagos's because its average delivery time is higher.

It can seem harmless to start the bars at some value other than 0 -- say at 20 minutes, to make small differences between cities stand out. That distorts the comparison. A bar chart is easy to read because the eye compares bar lengths from a common baseline, so the lengths themselves have to stay true to the values. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars that start at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall: Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0.

coverage.learning_objective: Create a box plot with matplotlib to visualize a numeric variable's quartiles, median, and outliers, optionally comparing several groups.

required_facts.statement: plt.boxplot(x) (or ax.boxplot(x)) draws a box plot from the data in x; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes.

The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers).
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.
Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as x draws one box for each array in the sequence; tick_labels=[...] labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare the full spread of delivery times across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- not just their averages, but how spread out and how extreme each city's times get. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

`plt.boxplot(x)` (or `ax.boxplot(x)`) draws a box plot from the data in `x`; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes. The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers). For example, if Lagos's box runs from Q1 = 20 minutes to Q3 = 30 minutes, the interquartile range (IQR) is the length of the box: 30 - 20 = 10 minutes. The whiskers can then reach at most 1.5 x 10 = 15 minutes beyond the box -- no lower than 5 minutes and no higher than 45 minutes -- so a 50-minute Lagos delivery would be drawn as a separate flier point.

Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as `x` draws one box for each array in the sequence; `tick_labels=[...]` labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value. `lagos_times = orders.loc[orders["city"] == "Lagos", "delivery_time_minutes"]` pulls out just the Lagos delivery times by boolean filtering, and `abuja_times`/`kano_times` are built the same way for the other two cities. `plt.boxplot([lagos_times, abuja_times, kano_times], tick_labels=["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"])` then draws three boxes side by side, one per city, each labeled with its city name instead of 1, 2, 3.

video_need.reason: The box/whisker anatomy -- which edge is Q1 versus Q3, where the median line sits, what counts as a whisker versus a flier point -- is a labeled-diagram concept that is far clearer pointed-to on an annotated drawing than described purely in words.

required_facts.statement: ax.set_xlabel('...') and ax.set_ylabel('...') set the x-axis and y-axis labels, and ax.set_title('...') sets the Axes title.
Passing label='...' to a plotting call (e.g. ax.plot(data, label='data1')) and then calling ax.legend() displays a legend identifying each labeled series.
In the pyplot interface, plt.xlabel(), plt.ylabel(), and plt.title() set the same label/title elements on the current Axes.

teaching_blocks.content: Titles, axis labels, and legends are the text that tells a reader what a plot shows. Matplotlib gives two parallel ways to add them, depending on whether you are working with an Axes object or the pyplot interface directly.

`ax.set_xlabel('...')` and `ax.set_ylabel('...')` set the x-axis and y-axis labels, and `ax.set_title('...')` sets the Axes title. `ax.set_xlabel("Day")`, `ax.set_ylabel("Average delivery time (minutes)")`, and `ax.set_title("Average delivery time by day")` label the Lagos trend line from before.

Passing `label='...'` to a plotting call (e.g. `ax.plot(data, label='data1')`) and then calling `ax.legend()` displays a legend identifying each labeled series. `days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` and `lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]` are the same 5 days of Lagos averages from before, so `ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label="Lagos")` followed by `ax.legend()` shows a legend identifying the Lagos line, which matters once a second city's line is added to the same Axes.

In the pyplot interface, `plt.xlabel()`, `plt.ylabel()`, and `plt.title()` set the same label/title elements on the current Axes -- the pyplot equivalents of `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()`.

context.concept_name: Matching chart type to the analytical question

coverage.learning_objective: Match a chart type (bar, histogram, line, scatter, or box) to the analytical question being explored during one's own analysis.

required_facts.statement: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories.
plt.hist() bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars.
Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis.
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

teaching_blocks.content: With five chart types available, the question during your own exploration is which one actually answers the question you're asking of the data.

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- average delivery time per city, for instance. `plt.hist()` bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars -- useful for how delivery times themselves are spread out. Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- average delivery time across the days of the week. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis -- whether distance and delivery time move together. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- the full spread of delivery times across several cities at once, not just their averages.

Picking a chart type during exploration comes down to naming what you're actually asking: a category comparison, a single variable's spread, a trend over time, a relationship between two variables, or a spread comparison across several groups.

video_need.reason: Walking through the same delivery dataset rendered as each candidate chart type, side by side, makes the decision process more concrete than the text's recap, though the recap of each chart's purpose already orients a learner.

teaching_blocks.content: Most plotting calls so far have needed you to pull a column or an array out of `orders` yourself before plotting it. Seaborn's plotting functions operate on dataframes and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot (for example `data=`, `x=`, `y=`) rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

`seaborn.barplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` visualizes an aggregate statistical estimate for each category as a bar; its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar by default. After `import seaborn as sns`, `sns.barplot(data=orders, x="city", y="delivery_time_minutes")` plots average delivery time per city directly from the `orders` DataFrame and its column names -- no separate `.groupby()` call needed first, and each bar comes with an error bar seaborn adds automatically.

teaching_blocks.content: `seaborn.set_theme()` accepts a `style` parameter (default `'darkgrid'`) and a `palette` parameter (default `'deep'`) among its arguments, which set the plot's background/gridline style and its color palette respectively. `sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="deep")` switches to a white background with gridlines.

`sns.set_theme(style=..., palette=...)` changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn. Because it works by changing global defaults, calling `sns.set_theme()` changes how plots drawn after that call look -- it does not go back and restyle a figure you already drew and displayed earlier.

context.concept_name: Basic A/B test structure (control vs treatment group)

coverage.learning_objective: Given a description of an experiment, identify its control group, its treatment group, and the metric being compared between them.

required_facts.statement: Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment.
Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control.

teaching_blocks.content: The delivery company wants to know whether a redesigned checkout button on its ordering app gets more people to complete an order. Rather than guess, it runs a controlled test on real users.

Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment. Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control. For the checkout button, the existing button is the control (A), the redesigned button is the treatment (B), users are randomly shown one or the other, and the metric compared is the share of each group that completes an order.
Every A/B test has these parts: a control group, a treatment group, and the measure being compared between them. The treatment group's result is then compared against the control, the baseline.

video_need.reason: Randomly splitting one population of users into two groups that each experience something different is a spatial/process relationship -- a diagram showing users being randomly routed into a control arm and a treatment arm makes the structure clearer than describing the split in words.

media.group_title: A/B test structure: two variants, one metric, one baseline

segments.label: Defining A/B test structure: control group, treatment group, and the metric tracked
segments.summary: A/B testing (also called split testing) grew out of randomized controlled trials. The core idea: show the new or varied version of a product to one sample of users — the experimental group — and the existing version to a separate sample — the control group. The difference in product performance between the two groups is then tracked over the test period. If the varied version underperforms, the business can decide whether to refine it or explore other directions.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the clip names the two groups and what gets measured. Note: the clip calls the treatment group the 'experimental group' — Devspace uses 'treatment group'.
bridge_note.after: The clip covers f3's structure but does not explain randomized assignment (f1, f2). The teaching text covers both.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a short description of an A/B test scenario, identify which group is the control, which is the treatment, and which metric is being compared between them.
practice_anchor.success: The learner correctly labels the control group (original/A), the treatment group (modified/B), and names the single metric used to compare the two groups, with no confusion between the two roles.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a population of users being randomly split into two arms — a control arm (original experience, A) and a treatment arm (modified experience, B) — with a metric arrow pointing from each arm to a comparison step, making the structure and the direction of comparison visible at a glance.

coverage.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the lift (percentage change) between a treatment group's result and a control group's result.

required_facts.statement: Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%.
Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

teaching_blocks.content: Once the checkout-button test has run, the raw numbers -- say, a 20% completion rate for the control button and a 22% completion rate for the redesigned one -- need to be turned into a comparison that's easy to talk about.

Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%. Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.

Applying that to the checkout test: a treatment rate of 22% over a control rate of 20% is a 2-percentage-point difference, which as a percentage of the 20% baseline is a 10% lift -- the same 10%-relative-improvement structure as the textbook example, just with the checkout numbers.

Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control). Lift puts the observed difference into one figure: a positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test, and a negative lift means it came out below.

video_need.reason: Lift is a percentage-change calculation on two numbers that are already known; the worked example fully shows how to compute and read it, with no mechanism, UI, or changing state to demonstrate.

practice_anchor.success: The function correctly computes lift as (treatment - control) / control * 100, returns a string that includes the numeric lift value and correctly labels the direction (positive, negative, or neutral) for at least three distinct input pairs.

context.concept_name: Conceptual effect of sample size on confidence

coverage.learning_objective: Given two results with the same estimate but different sample sizes, explain why the estimate from the larger sample is more trustworthy.

required_facts.statement: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample.

The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable on the response; in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two versions of the checkout-button test both come back showing the same 10% lift -- but one ran with 50 users in each group and the other ran with 5,000 users in each group. Should you trust them equally?

A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample. The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable (here, which button a user saw) on the response (whether they completed an order); in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

So the 5,000-user version of the checkout test tends to provide a more precise estimate of the button's effect than the 50-user version, even though both happened to show the same 10% lift -- the larger test observed far more cases, so it can estimate the button's effect on completed orders more accurately.

video_need.reason: The idea that small-sample estimates scatter more widely around the true effect than large-sample ones is a spread that's easier to picture with a diagram of estimates clustering tightly for the large sample and spreading widely for the small one than to hold in mind from a description alone.

practice_anchor.objective: Given two A/B tests on the same checkout-button change — one with 50 users per group and one with 5,000 users per group — both showing a 10% lift, explain in writing which result is more trustworthy and why, referencing precision of estimation and number of cases observed.
practice_anchor.success: The learner correctly identifies the 5,000-user test as more trustworthy, explains that a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate, and states that observing more cases allows a more accurate estimate of the button's effect on completed orders.

visual_anchor.purpose: Side-by-side display of two groups of estimated lift values — one cluster tight around 10% (large sample) and one scattered widely around 10% (small sample) — making visible that small-sample estimates vary more around the true effect than large-sample ones.

context.concept_name: Conceptual interpretation of statistical significance/confidence level

coverage.learning_objective: Given a result reported with a significance or confidence figure, explain what that figure does and doesn't tell you about the underlying effect.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true; it is used to quantify the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.

Statistical significance is a measure of how unusual an experiment's results would be if there were actually no difference in performance between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to random chance alone.

A confidence interval represents a range of plausible values where we are likely to find the population parameter; if many samples were taken and a 95% confidence interval were built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain the parameter.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant.

misconceptions.statement: Not every confidence interval captures the true population proportion: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion, showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it even when the method is followed correctly.

teaching_blocks.content: The checkout test showed a 10% lift for the redesigned button. Before recommending it company-wide, you need language for how sure that result actually is.

The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration. For the checkout test, H0 would be that the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate, and HA would be that it does.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true -- it quantifies the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. Statistical significance measures how unusual a result would be if there were actually no difference between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to chance alone.

A confidence interval is a range of plausible values likely to contain the population parameter (the true value you are trying to estimate); if many samples were taken and a 95% interval built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain it.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval. So it's not quite right to say "there's a 95% chance the true completion-rate difference is in this interval" -- the 95% describes how the method behaves across many samples, not the probability attached to this one interval.

Not every confidence interval captures the true value, even when the method is followed correctly: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion -- showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it. The same is true of any single confidence interval you compute for a result like the checkout test.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant. A large enough checkout test could detect a tiny, practically unimportant lift and call it statistically significant -- significance tells you how unusual the result would be if there were truly no difference, not that the lift is big enough to matter.

video_need.reason: Hypotheses, p-values, and confidence intervals are all defined in terms of what would happen across many repeated samples -- an animation showing repeated samples each producing their own interval, most catching the true value and a few missing it, makes that repeated-sampling idea concrete in a way that a single static definition can't.

media.group_title: How p-values work and why a small p-value doesn't mean a large effect

segments.label: P-values, statistical significance, and the limits of a small p-value
segments.summary: Using a drug-comparison scenario, the clip builds up from a single-person trial to a large-sample experiment to show why we need many observations before drawing conclusions. It introduces the p-value as a way to quantify how confident we can be that two groups differ, explains the 0.05 threshold in terms of false positives (getting a significant result when there is actually no difference), and names the null hypothesis as the assumption that the two drugs are the same. It closes by showing that a larger sample can produce a smaller p-value for a one-point difference than a smaller sample produces for a six-point difference — demonstrating that a small p-value does not imply a large effect.

The clip does not cover confidence intervals (f4, f5) or the misconception about interval capture (m1) — the text covers those.
bridge_note.after: The clip confirms that significance measures unusualness under no-difference, not the size of the effect. Confidence intervals, the repeated-sampling interpretation, and the interval-capture misconception are covered only in the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a result reported as 'significant at 95% confidence', write a plain-language explanation that correctly states what the confidence level means (how the method behaves across many samples) and explicitly rules out two common misreadings: that the result is practically important, and that there is a 95% probability the true value lies in this specific interval.
practice_anchor.success: The explanation correctly attributes the 95% to the long-run behaviour of the method, not to a probability attached to the single interval; it notes that statistical significance does not imply practical importance; and it does not claim the interval is guaranteed to contain the true value.

context.concept_name: Drawing a business conclusion from an experiment-result summary

coverage.learning_objective: Given an experiment's results, state a business conclusion that follows from the data without overreaching beyond what the numbers show.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

In one hypothesis-test example, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

In a second example, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value.

While we failed to reject the null hypothesis in the first example, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but we were not able to detect it with the relatively small sample of 50.

misconceptions.statement: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

teaching_blocks.content: Getting a p-value or confidence interval isn't the end of the job -- someone still has to decide what to do about the checkout button.

As before, H0 often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and HA an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

Consider two textbook examples, each testing whether a proportion equals a null value of 0.333. In one, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. In a second, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.

While the first example failed to reject the null hypothesis, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but it could not be detected with the relatively small sample of 50. Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

Analyzing a test's results means saying whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect versus the baseline (control). For the checkout test, that means stating plainly whether the redesigned button did better, worse, or about the same as the original -- not just reporting a p-value and stopping. If the checkout test's summary showed its null value inside the confidence interval, the conclusion would be that the data did not provide sufficient evidence of a difference -- not that the new button makes no difference.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value. A business conclusion has to weigh that: a statistically significant lift on the checkout button might still be too small to have any practical value, so look at the size of the lift, not just whether it was detected.

video_need.reason: The two contrasting outcomes -- a null value sitting inside a confidence interval versus falling outside it -- are easier to place and compare with a number-line diagram showing the interval and where the null value lands than to hold in mind from the worked numbers alone.

media.group_title: When statistical significance misleads: the sample-size effect

segments.label: Large samples can make trivially small differences statistically significant
segments.summary: The instructor explains that statistical significance is tightly linked to sample size: with n = 10, sample means of 10.05, 10.1, and 10.2 all produce large p-values and no evidence against the null; with n = 5,000 and identical sample means, the p-values become tiny and the same differences are called highly significant. The key point is that a tiny p-value only tells you the observed difference was unlikely under the null — it says nothing about whether a difference of 0.1 matters in practice. Whether the result has any practical importance is a separate question for domain experts.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the same three sample means flip from 'no evidence' to 'highly significant' just by changing n. The clip uses mu and box plots; Devspace's running example uses a proportion and a checkout button.
bridge_note.after: The clip covers f5 only. The text also covers the null-value/confidence-interval logic (f1–f3), the fail-to-reject misconception (f6, m1), and what a business conclusion must state (f4).

practice_anchor.objective: Given an A/B test summary card — showing the control conversion rate, the treatment conversion rate, the 95% confidence interval for the difference, and the null value — arrange the four reasoning steps in the correct order: (1) locate the null value relative to the confidence interval, (2) state the reject/fail-to-reject decision, (3) correct the fail-to-reject misconception if applicable, (4) write the plain-language business conclusion including whether the lift has practical value.
practice_anchor.success: The learner places all four steps in the correct sequence and writes a business conclusion that names the direction of the effect (or absence of evidence for one), does not claim the null is true when failing to reject, and flags whether a detected lift is large enough to matter practically.

visual_anchor.purpose: A number-line diagram showing a 95% confidence interval as a shaded band, with two scenarios side by side: one where the null value (p0 = 0.333) falls inside the interval (fail to reject) and one where it falls outside and below the interval (reject, conclude lower) — making the contrast between the two textbook examples immediately visible.

context.concept_name: Identifying the business decision a stakeholder needs the analysis to inform

coverage.learning_objective: Identify the business decision that a stakeholder's analysis request is meant to inform.

required_facts.statement: Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making.
The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions.

teaching_blocks.content: An operations manager emails you: "Can you look into our delivery times?" Before opening a notebook, the first thing worth asking is not what to measure, but what decision this is actually for.

Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making. A request for analysis often exists because someone needs to decide something, even when the request itself doesn't say so directly.

The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions. For the delivery-times request, that can mean asking the manager directly: is this about deciding whether to hire more couriers for the Lagos route, whether to renegotiate with a courier partner, or something else? The answer changes what you'd actually need to measure.

Naming the decision up front -- "this analysis is meant to help decide whether to add Lagos couriers" -- gives everything that follows a target to aim at, rather than leaving you to guess what "look into it" was supposed to produce.

video_need.reason: This is a reasoning habit conveyed through a worked request-to-decision example in prose; there is no diagram, code, or process to watch.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a vague stakeholder request, state the specific decision it is meant to inform.
practice_anchor.success: The learner produces a single sentence naming the underlying decision (e.g. 'This analysis is meant to help decide whether to renegotiate with the courier partner'), not a restatement of the request or a list of metrics.

teaching_notes: Opens the stakeholder-communication thread's running scenario: an operations manager's delivery-times request, carried through later concepts in this tile group.

context.concept_name: Stating a finding precisely and quantitatively (the specific number or comparison, not a vague claim)

coverage.learning_objective: State an analysis finding as a specific, complete claim that accurately reflects what the data shows, rather than a vague summary.

required_facts.statement: A communication's big idea must articulate a unique point of view, convey what's at stake, and be a complete sentence.

A claim about the data should be checked against what the data actually shows, and narrowed if needed; one article's example revises the broader claim 'Price has declined for all products' to the more precise 'the average retail price of existing products declined' once the underlying data was examined more closely.
Writing about data should be specific about the point being made.

Putting data into context includes making comparisons, for example: 'There were 787,000 suspensions in the 2022/23 academic year. This is an increase from the previous year, when 578,300 suspensions occurred...'

teaching_blocks.content: Once you've analyzed the delivery data, "delivery times went up" is a finding of sorts, but it doesn't say by how much, where, or compared to what.

A communication's big idea must articulate a unique point of view, convey what's at stake, and be a complete sentence -- not a fragment or a topic label. "Lagos delivery times" is only a topic label. "Lagos delivery times have risen, so customers on that route are waiting longer for their orders" is a complete sentence that takes a position (Lagos has slowed down) and says what's at stake (customers waiting longer).

A claim about the data should be checked against what the data actually shows, and narrowed if needed; one article's example revises the broader claim "Price has declined for all products" to the more precise "the average retail price of existing products declined" once the underlying data was examined more closely. The same check applies to the delivery claim: if only Lagos routes actually slowed down, "delivery times went up" should narrow to "Lagos delivery times went up", not describe every city.

Writing about data should be specific about the point being made, and putting data into context includes making comparisons -- for example: "There were 787,000 suspensions in the 2022/23 academic year. This is an increase from the previous year, when 578,300 suspensions occurred..." Following that same pattern, a precise delivery finding names the number and the comparison: "the average Lagos delivery time rose to 30 minutes this month, up from 22 minutes last month," rather than just "delivery times went up."

video_need.reason: Precision in a written claim is demonstrated by rewriting a vague sentence into a specific one -- a text-and-example skill with no visual component.

practice_anchor.objective: Rewrite the vague finding 'sales went up' as a precise, quantified statement that names a specific number and a comparison to a prior period.
practice_anchor.success: The rewritten statement is a complete sentence, names at least one specific number, and includes a comparison (e.g., to a previous month or year), with no vague qualitative language remaining.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a vague finding sentence alongside its rewritten precise version so the learner can see exactly what changes when a number and comparison are added.

teaching_notes: Optional enrichment (quality assurance of communications, f1) is skipped -- not required for this concept's coverage.

context.concept_name: Converting a vague business question into a specific, measurable analytical question

coverage.learning_objective: Convert a vague business question into a specific analytical question with agreed boundaries and precision, that can actually be answered with data.

required_facts.statement: In the engagement and scoping stage, the analyst should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, the context, and the boundaries of the analysis, as well as constraints such as deadlines and available resources.
The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work, including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error.

A well-formed statistical question makes clear the variable(s) of interest, the group it focuses on, and its intent — describing the data, comparing a variable across two or more groups, or looking at an association between two variables — and can be answered with data collected or already in hand.

teaching_blocks.content: "Are deliveries going well?" is the kind of question a stakeholder might actually ask -- and it can't be answered with data as written.

In the engagement and scoping stage, the analyst should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, the context, and the boundaries of the analysis, as well as constraints such as deadlines and available resources. That kind of conversation can turn "are deliveries going well" into something answerable: which cities, which time period, compared against what.
