teaching_blocks.content: During your own exploration, you might have built a bar chart, a line plot, and a box plot of the delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which one actually makes the Lagos point, for this audience?

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- showing average delivery time side by side across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- showing Lagos delivery time rising week over week. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- but a boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve, so choosing a different display altogether may avoid confusion for audiences who do not know this chart type or how to read it; for a manager who hasn't seen a box plot before, the bar chart or line plot can often make the point more directly.

A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data, and is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%). If the point is "Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume," a pie chart of each city's share of total orders fits that part-to-whole framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience -- useful to keep in mind if the distance/delivery-time relationship ever needs to go in front of the manager directly, rather than staying an exploratory chart.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths, since both show a value at a glance -- but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye.

context.concept_name: Defining a capstone business question/problem statement

coverage.learning_objective: Define a specific business question or problem statement for a chosen dataset, so the question itself gives every later capstone step (retrieval, cleaning, analysis) a concrete target to serve.

required_facts.statement: Before analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified.
Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the operations team at a courier company comes to you with a vague complaint: deliveries feel slow lately, can you look into it? That request isn't yet something you can analyze. Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified.

Turning that complaint into a workable target is called scoping. Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

For the courier company, scoping the vague complaint means settling its context and boundaries: which orders (a specific quarter's deliveries), which measure (delivery time against a target), and which unit of comparison (delivery zone). The result is a specific business question: 'Which delivery zones are missing the delivery-time target, and by how much, over the last quarter?' That question already carries a context (this company's last quarter of orders) and boundaries (zones and delivery time, not every possible cause of delay), so you and the operations team share the same understanding of what the analysis will and won't answer.
Every later capstone step -- what data to retrieve, how to clean it, what to compute -- serves this one sentence. Scope it loosely, and the rest of the project has nothing precise to aim at.

video_need.reason: Turning a vague complaint into a specific, bounded question is a reasoning step, not a process with moving parts. A short recap slide of the before/after question is enough; the text already walks through the scoping itself.

context.concept_name: Selecting an appropriate data retrieval method (SQL and/or spreadsheet)

coverage.learning_objective: Given the capstone dataset and where it is stored, choose and justify whether to retrieve it with a SQL query, a spreadsheet import, or both.

required_facts.statement: Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval.
read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame.

teaching_blocks.content: With the question scoped, the next decision is how to get the data. This capstone's order records live in the courier company's SQL database (an orders table), while the driver roster is kept in an Excel workbook.

Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval. So the orders table, sitting in the company's database, is a SQL-query job.
read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame. So the driver roster workbook, which never touches a database, is a read_excel() job instead.

The capstone ends up using both: a SQL query pulls the last quarter's orders (zone, driver_id, delivery_time) from the orders table, and read_excel() pulls the driver roster (driver_id, name, zone, shift) from the spreadsheet. Two different sources, matched to two different retrieval tools.

It can look like everything should go through one tool, but the method follows where each source actually sits: the orders table lives in the company's database, so a SQL query retrieves it, while the driver roster is an Excel workbook, so read_excel() reads it into a DataFrame.
Matching each source to its retrieval tool -- SQL query for the database, read_excel() for the workbook -- is the first executable step of the workflow, before any cleaning or analysis starts.

required_facts.statement: An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results; a phase such as scoping or design may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (for example via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements (such as cleaning) focused as early as possible.
source_refs: uk_gov_data_quality_framework#3.1 Assess data quality at all stages of the lifecycle

required_facts.statement: Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver (the people who need them); activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations.

teaching_blocks.content: With the question scoped and both retrieval tools chosen, sketch the whole project's shape before touching either one.

An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results; a phase such as scoping or design may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. For the capstone: scope the question, retrieve, clean/model, analyze, visualize, and communicate -- and if, say, cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope the question rather than pressing on.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (for example via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements such as cleaning focused as early as possible. So right after the orders query and the roster import, the capstone checks for problems like missing delivery times, rather than waiting until the final analysis to discover them.

Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables. The capstone's orders and drivers are two such tables, so a modeling stage links them before any deeper analysis relies on both together.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver -- the people who need them; activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations. The capstone's version of this is reporting the zone-delay findings back to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

Scope, retrieve, clean/model, analyze, visualize, communicate -- with quality checked throughout and any stage open to revisiting -- is the shape every remaining capstone concept fills in one piece at a time.

context.concept_name: Integrating SQL querying into an end-to-end project

coverage.learning_objective: Combine already-learned SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY into one SQL query that retrieves the specific rows, columns, and groups the capstone's business question needs.

required_facts.statement: A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied.

teaching_blocks.content: The first executable step of the workflow is retrieving last quarter's orders with SQL.

A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query. In the capstone, that means the orders query can filter down to last quarter's rows and group the result by zone in one statement, rather than as separate steps.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied. In the capstone, that means the orders and drivers tables can be joined in the same FROM clause, before the WHERE and GROUP BY narrow and group the combined rows.

Combined, the capstone's retrieval query looks like: SELECT o.zone, AVG(o.delivery_time) FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-07-01' GROUP BY o.zone; -- the join combines each order with its matching driver row first, the WHERE clause then narrows the rows to last quarter (April 1 to June 30), and the GROUP BY groups what's left by zone, so AVG gives one average delivery time per zone.
None of this is new SQL syntax -- it's the same SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY already learned, aimed at the capstone's own question.

video_need.reason: Watching the joined, filtered, grouped query actually run and return zone-level rows helps confirm the clause ordering, though the text's worked query already shows the full combination.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary.
COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]…) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met.

teaching_blocks.content: For part of the analysis, the driver roster's shift and zone details are paired with each order's delivery_time in one sheet, so that step runs in spreadsheet tools instead of SQL.

A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, that means the delivery sheet's zone and shift fields default into Rows while delivery_time defaults into Values, ready to be rearranged into a more useful layout.

COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]...) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met. In the capstone, that means counting how many deliveries in a specific zone exceeded a time threshold, using the zone and the time as the two criteria.

For the capstone's delivery sheet, where each row pairs an order's zone and delivery_time with its driver's shift from the roster: selecting the data range, inserting a PivotTable and adding those fields puts zone and shift -- both non-numeric -- in Rows by default, and delivery_time, which is numeric, in Values. Dragging shift from Rows to Columns rearranges the summary into a zone-by-shift grid, and changing the Values field's summary function to Average makes each cell an average delivery time. Separately, COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45") counts how many Ikeja deliveries in the sheet took more than 45 minutes, since both criteria -- the zone and the time threshold -- must be met at once.
The PivotTable and COUNTIFS skills already learned are now run on this project's own roster and delivery data instead of a practice file.

context.concept_name: Integrating Python/pandas cleaning and analysis into an end-to-end project

coverage.learning_objective: Apply already-learned pandas cleaning (isna/dropna/fillna) and analysis (groupby aggregation) to the capstone's own retrieved dataset.

required_facts.statement: isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column.

teaching_blocks.content: Once orders and roster are both retrieved, pandas is where they get cleaned and combined for the actual analysis.

isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value. In the capstone, that means flagging which of the retrieved orders are missing a delivery_time before deciding whether to drop or fill those rows.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column. In the capstone, that means splitting the cleaned orders by zone and reducing each zone's delivery times to one summary number.

On the capstone's retrieved orders, orders['delivery_time'].isna() flags rows with no delivery time recorded; those rows get removed with dropna() (or, where a default makes sense, filled with fillna()). Then orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() splits the cleaned orders by zone, computes the mean delivery time independently within each zone, and combines the per-zone results into one summary -- an aggregation, since each zone group is reduced to a single number.
The same isna()/dropna()/fillna() and groupby skills already learned are now run on the capstone's own retrieved data instead of a practice dataset.

context.concept_name: Building a data model for the capstone dataset

coverage.learning_objective: Connect the capstone project's own tables using the correct primary keys, foreign keys, and one-to-many relationships.

required_facts.statement: A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

teaching_blocks.content: The capstone's data spans two tables -- Orders and Drivers -- so before deeper analysis relies on both together, they need to be modeled as related tables.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references. In the capstone, that means the Drivers table needs a column that uniquely identifies each driver, and the Orders table needs a column whose values must match one of those driver identifiers.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table. In the capstone, that means one driver can appear in many orders, the same one-to-many pattern as one customer having many orders.

Mapped onto the capstone: Drivers has driver_id as its primary key, uniquely identifying each driver row. Orders has its own primary key, order_id, plus a driver_id column that is a foreign key -- its values must match a driver_id that already exists in Drivers. Since one driver delivers many orders, this is a one-to-many relationship: one row on the Drivers ('one') side relates to many rows on the Orders ('many') side, the same pattern as CustID sitting in the Order table and matching a valid CustID in the Customer table.
Getting the primary key/foreign key pairing right connects the two tables correctly before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted.

context.concept_name: Applying descriptive statistics to capstone findings

coverage.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the descriptive statistics (using pandas) that support the capstone project's business question.

required_facts.statement: describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful.

teaching_blocks.content: With cleaned, modeled data, the business question needs actual numbers: how late are deliveries, by zone?

describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame. In the capstone, that means running describe() on a zone's delivery_time column to get that summary in one call.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful. In the capstone, that means checking whether a handful of unusually long deliveries are skewing a zone's average before trusting it as typical.

Running describe() on one zone's delivery_time column returns a mean of 52 minutes, with the median (the middle quartile in describe()'s output) at 38 minutes. But a handful of deliveries in that zone took over three hours -- a stalled vehicle, a wrong address -- and the mean is pulled up by those extreme observations, while the median, more robust to them, stays at 38 minutes. The capstone's business question is which zones are missing the delivery-time target and by how much, which calls for judging a typical delivery against that target rather than one skewed by a few rare extremes, so the median is the more useful number here.
describe() gives the full summary; deciding whether the mean or the median actually answers the business question depends on whether extreme values are skewing that particular column.

teaching_blocks.content: With the plan, retrieval, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and visualization steps all defined, what's left is carrying the whole thing out yourself, end to end, without being walked through each step again.

During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed. For the capstone, the workflow outline from earlier becomes that analytical plan, and it's normal to adjust it once the SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas work actually starts.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained. So as the capstone's query, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and figures get built, a short record of what was decided -- for example, how missing delivery times were handled -- is kept alongside a check that the results still answer the original zone-delay question.
Independent execution is running the whole plan yourself, adjusting it as needed, and keeping a record of the decisions made along the way -- not any single new tool.

Designing a communication with a specific person in mind, even if that isn't always the reality, can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group; knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms. So instead of writing for 'the ops team' in general, the capstone summary is written as if for the Head of Operations specifically, framing the zone-delay finding around what would motivate that person -- meeting the delivery-time target.

A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end: the beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context, the middle presents what the analysis found, and the ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step. For the capstone, that means opening with the courier company and last quarter's delivery-time target, then the finding that certain zones are missing it and by how much, then closing with a recommended next step -- though depending on the audience and relationship, that recommendation can instead be placed up front for a Head of Operations who prefers the bottom line first.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements; this communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations. For the capstone, that means the finished summary pack should let the Head of Operations judge for themselves whether it actually answers the zone-delay question they raised, not just report that the analysis was done.
A narrated summary aimed at one specific person, moving through beginning, middle, and end, is what turns the capstone's findings into something its audience can actually use.

clusters.title: Datasets and Variable Types
clusters.reasoning: Rows/columns and variable types are two facets of the same foundational idea — what a dataset looks like and what kind of values it holds. A learner encounters both simultaneously when first opening a dataset. Neither requires the other as a prerequisite; they read as complementary parts of one orientation.

clusters.title: Data Quality and the Analysis Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Data quality is a prerequisite concern that feeds directly into the analysis workflow — understanding what makes data trustworthy is part of understanding the workflow itself. These two concepts read as steps of one process. Ethics/privacy is a distinct conceptual domain (legal and ethical obligations) that learners must learn to separate from the technical workflow, so it is not clustered here.

clusters.title: Variables and Core Data Types
clusters.reasoning: Variable assignment and core data types are inseparable in Python: every assignment creates a typed value. Learners encounter both in the same first code cell. They read as two aspects of one idea — naming and typing values.

clusters.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
clusters.reasoning: Comparison and logical operators are always used together to build compound conditions (e.g., x > 0 and x < 10). They form one idea: constructing boolean tests. Arithmetic operators produce numbers rather than booleans and are a distinct concept; type_conversion is a separate operation. Clustering only comparison and logical keeps the important boundary between numeric and boolean operations visible.

clusters.title: Lists, Dictionaries, and Tuples
clusters.reasoning: Lists, dictionaries, and tuples are Python's three core built-in collection types. Showing them together makes the key distinctions immediately visible: lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, dictionaries are key-value mappings. Learners need to choose between them in practice, and the contrast is the core learning. They read as three variants of one idea: storing multiple values in Python.

clusters.title: Conditionals and For Loops
clusters.reasoning: Conditionals and for loops are the two foundational control flow structures in Python, and they are routinely combined (a for loop containing an if statement). They read as complementary parts of one idea: directing program flow. Neither requires the other as a prerequisite at the tile's start.

clusters.title: While Loops and Loop Control
clusters.reasoning: Loop control statements (break, continue, pass) are only meaningful inside a loop. While loops and loop control read as one idea: how to run and exit a loop conditionally. They are always taught together.

clusters.title: Comprehensions and Iterating Collections
clusters.reasoning: List comprehensions are a compact syntax for iterating over a collection and transforming it — they are the same idea expressed differently. Showing them together lets learners see the equivalence between a for-loop iteration and a comprehension, which is the core insight of this tile.

clusters.title: Defining Functions, Parameters, and Return Values
clusters.reasoning: Defining a function, passing parameters, and returning values are the three inseparable parts of a function's basic interface. A learner cannot understand any one of them without the other two — they form a single mental model: 'a function takes inputs and produces an output.' Default/keyword arguments are a parameter variant that builds on this foundation and is better shown separately. Variable scope is a distinct concept about name resolution.

clusters.title: Measures of Center and Spread
clusters.reasoning: Measures of center (mean, median, mode) and measures of spread (variance, standard deviation, IQR) are the two complementary halves of descriptive statistics — they answer 'where is the data?' and 'how spread out is it?' respectively. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: summarizing a distribution numerically.

clusters.title: Distribution Shape, Outliers, and Frequency Distributions
clusters.reasoning: Reading a frequency distribution, identifying its shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), and reasoning about outliers are three steps of one analytical act: understanding how a variable is distributed. A learner cannot reason about outliers without first understanding shape, and shape is read from a frequency distribution. They form a single workflow and are always taught together.

clusters.title: Correlation and Its Limits
clusters.reasoning: Correlation, how to interpret the correlation coefficient, and the correlation-vs-causation caveat are three aspects of one concept. A learner who knows what correlation is but not how to interpret r, or who doesn't know the causation caveat, has an incomplete and potentially dangerous understanding. Showing them together as a cluster makes the complete picture visible while keeping each sub-concept individually addressable.

clusters.title: DataFrames, Series, and Reading Data
clusters.reasoning: The DataFrame/Series model is the conceptual foundation for all pandas work, and reading data (pd.read_csv) is the first operation that produces a DataFrame. A learner needs the model to understand what read_csv returns. These two concepts are the entry point to pandas and read as one idea: what a DataFrame is and how to get one.

clusters.title: Creating and Inspecting DataFrames
clusters.reasoning: Creating a DataFrame and inspecting it (head, info, describe, shape) are the first two steps of every pandas workflow — you create or load data, then immediately examine it. They read as a single orientation step: 'make a DataFrame and look at it.'

clusters.title: Selecting and Filtering Data
clusters.reasoning: loc/iloc (label/position-based selection) and boolean filtering (condition-based selection) are the two primary ways to select subsets of a DataFrame. Showing them together makes the contrast clear: one selects by address, the other by condition. They are variants of one operation — subsetting data — and learners need both to work effectively.

clusters.title: Type Conversion and Datetime Handling
clusters.reasoning: dtype conversion (astype, pd.to_numeric) and datetime handling (pd.to_datetime, dt accessor) are both about correcting column types in a DataFrame. Datetime conversion is the most common and complex type conversion case. They read as two aspects of one task: making sure columns have the right type before analysis.

clusters.title: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
clusters.reasoning: String cleaning, removing duplicates, and handling missing values are the three main data cleaning operations in pandas. They address different problems but are always applied in the same cleaning phase of an analysis workflow. Showing them as a cluster lets learners see the full cleaning toolkit at once, with each operation individually addressable.

clusters.title: Mapping and Applying Transformations
clusters.reasoning: map (for substituting values via a dictionary or function on a Series) and apply (for applying a function element-wise or row/column-wise) are two variants of the same idea: transforming values in a DataFrame. Showing them together makes the distinction clear — map is for simple substitution, apply is for custom logic.

clusters.title: Concatenating and Merging DataFrames
clusters.reasoning: concat (stacking DataFrames by rows or columns) and merge (joining DataFrames on a key) are the two ways to combine DataFrames in pandas. Showing them together makes the fundamental distinction clear: concat stacks, merge joins. They are variants of one operation — combining DataFrames — and learners need to choose between them in practice.

clusters.title: The Relational Model and SELECT Basics
clusters.reasoning: The relational model (tables, rows, columns, relationships) is the conceptual foundation for SQL, and SELECT is the first query that retrieves from it. A learner needs the model to understand what SELECT returns. These two concepts are the entry point to SQL and read as one idea: what a relational database is and how to query it.

clusters.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE and Logical Operators
clusters.reasoning: WHERE and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) are inseparable in practice — every non-trivial WHERE clause uses logical operators to combine conditions. They read as one idea: constructing a row filter. NULL handling involves three-valued logic (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) which is a distinct and often surprising concept that learners must understand on its own terms, so it is not clustered here.

clusters.title: Sorting and Limiting Results
clusters.reasoning: ORDER BY and LIMIT/OFFSET are always used together to sort a result set and then take a slice of it (e.g., 'top 10 by revenue'). They read as two parts of one idea: controlling which rows appear in the output and in what order.

clusters.title: Aggregating Data with GROUP BY
clusters.reasoning: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG), GROUP BY, and HAVING are the three components of the SQL aggregation pattern. GROUP BY groups rows, aggregate functions summarize each group, and HAVING filters the groups. A learner cannot use any one of them effectively without understanding the others — they form a single mental model: 'group rows and summarize each group, optionally filtering groups.'

clusters.title: Text and Date Functions
clusters.reasoning: String functions (UPPER, LOWER, TRIM, SUBSTRING, CONCAT) and date/time functions (DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT, DATEDIFF) are both categories of scalar functions that transform column values in SELECT. They are often used together in data cleaning and reporting queries. Type casting (CAST, ::) is a distinct operation about converting between data types and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Entities, Tables, and Primary Keys
clusters.reasoning: Entities/tables and primary keys are inseparable in the relational model — a primary key is what uniquely identifies each row in a table and makes it a proper entity. A learner cannot understand what a table represents without understanding primary keys. They read as two aspects of one idea: what a table is and how rows are identified.

clusters.title: Foreign Keys and One-to-Many Relationships
clusters.reasoning: Foreign keys are the mechanism that implements one-to-many relationships — a foreign key in the 'many' table points to the primary key in the 'one' table. These two concepts are two sides of the same coin: the relationship pattern and the column that enforces it. They are always taught together in data modeling.

clusters.title: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
clusters.reasoning: Normalization (reducing redundancy by splitting data into related tables) and many-to-many junction tables (the normalization technique for many-to-many relationships) are tightly linked. A junction table is the canonical example of normalization in action. They read as two aspects of one idea: how to structure data to avoid redundancy.

clusters.title: Query Execution Order and Subqueries in WHERE
clusters.reasoning: SQL clause execution order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) directly explains why subqueries can appear in WHERE: the subquery runs first, producing a value that WHERE can filter on. Understanding execution order is the prerequisite mental model for understanding subquery placement. These two concepts read as one idea: how SQL processes a query and how that enables subqueries.

clusters.title: Subqueries in FROM and Common Table Expressions
clusters.reasoning: Subqueries in FROM (derived tables) and CTEs (WITH clause) are two syntactic approaches to the same idea: creating a named intermediate result set that the outer query can reference. CTEs are the modern, more readable alternative to subqueries in FROM. Showing them together makes the equivalence and the trade-offs immediately clear.

clusters.title: The Spreadsheet Grid and Cell References
clusters.reasoning: The spreadsheet grid model (rows, columns, cells) and cell references/ranges (A1, B2:D5) are inseparable — cell references are the addressing system for the grid. A learner cannot write a formula without understanding both. They read as two aspects of one foundational idea: how a spreadsheet is structured and how to point to locations in it.

clusters.title: Structured Tables and Named Ranges
clusters.reasoning: Structured tables (Excel Tables / Google Sheets tables with auto-expanding references) and named ranges are both mechanisms for giving a data region a meaningful name that can be referenced in formulas. They read as two variants of one idea: naming data regions to make formulas more readable and maintainable.

clusters.title: Sorting and Filtering Data
clusters.reasoning: Sorting (reordering rows by a column) and filtering (showing only rows that match a condition) are the two basic data exploration operations in a spreadsheet. They are always taught together and are often used in sequence: filter to a subset, then sort within it. They read as two parts of one idea: navigating and exploring tabular data.

clusters.title: Removing Duplicates and Splitting Text
clusters.reasoning: Removing duplicates and splitting text (Text to Columns / SPLIT) are both data cleaning operations applied to raw imported data. They are often used in sequence when cleaning a dataset: split combined fields, then remove duplicate rows. Cross-sheet references are a formula navigation concept and belong to a different idea.

clusters.title: Writing Formulas and Reference Types
clusters.reasoning: Formula syntax (= sign, operators, function calls) and relative/absolute references ($A$1 vs A1) are inseparable — every formula uses references, and whether those references are relative or absolute determines how the formula behaves when copied. They read as two aspects of one idea: how to write a formula correctly.

clusters.title: Text Combining and Text Extraction
clusters.reasoning: Text combining (CONCAT, TEXTJOIN, &) and text extraction (LEFT, RIGHT, MID, FIND) are two complementary text manipulation operations — one builds strings from parts, the other pulls parts from strings. They are variants of one idea: working with text values in formulas, and are often used together when cleaning or reformatting text data.

clusters.title: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH
clusters.reasoning: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH are the two main lookup approaches in spreadsheets. Showing them together makes the trade-offs immediately clear: VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP is simpler but limited to left-to-right lookups; INDEX/MATCH is more flexible. Learners need to choose between them in practice. Formula error troubleshooting is a debugging skill that applies to all formulas and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Building and Summarizing Pivot Tables
clusters.reasoning: Building a pivot table (inserting, configuring rows/columns/values) and summarizing with it (choosing aggregation functions, filtering, grouping) are two steps of one workflow. A learner cannot summarize with a pivot table without first building one. They read as the setup and the use of the same tool.

clusters.title: Figures, Layout, and Basic Plotting
clusters.reasoning: The Figure/Axes model, figure size and layout configuration, and basic pyplot plotting are three aspects of the same setup: creating a matplotlib figure. A learner needs all three to produce their first plot. They read as the initialization steps of any matplotlib visualization and are always taught together.

clusters.title: Bar Charts and Histograms
clusters.reasoning: Bar charts (categorical comparison) and histograms (continuous distribution) are often confused because they look similar. Showing them together makes the critical distinction immediately visible: bar charts have gaps between bars and compare categories; histograms have no gaps and show distribution. The contrast is the core learning, making them ideal for a cluster.

clusters.title: Line Plots and Scatter Plots
clusters.reasoning: Line plots (trends over an ordered axis, typically time) and scatter plots (relationship between two continuous variables) are both two-variable charts that learners often conflate. Showing them together makes the distinction clear: line plots connect ordered points to show trend; scatter plots show correlation between unordered pairs. Box plots show distribution rather than relationships and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Seaborn DataFrame Plotting and Statistical Functions
clusters.reasoning: Seaborn's DataFrame-aware plotting (sns.barplot, sns.scatterplot) and its statistical functions (sns.histplot with kde, sns.regplot, sns.boxplot) are two levels of the same library: basic chart creation and statistically-enhanced chart creation. They read as two aspects of one idea: using seaborn to visualize data. Themes and palettes are a styling concern that applies after the chart is created.

clusters.title: A/B Test Structure and Lift
clusters.reasoning: A/B test structure (control vs treatment, random assignment, metric selection) and lift interpretation (the relative improvement of treatment over control) are two aspects of the same experiment: how to design it and how to read its primary result. A learner cannot interpret lift without understanding the test structure that produced it.

clusters.title: Sample Size, Effect Size, and Statistical Significance
clusters.reasoning: Sample size/effect size and statistical significance/confidence intervals are two interconnected statistical concepts for evaluating experiment validity. Sample size determines whether an effect can be detected; significance tells you whether the detected effect is likely real. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: 'is this result trustworthy?' Business conclusions from experiments are the translation step that applies these concepts to a decision, and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Identifying Decisions, Findings, and Requirements
clusters.reasoning: Identifying the decision need, stating findings precisely, framing the analytical question, and identifying requirements are four sequential steps of the same pre-analysis phase: understanding what the stakeholder actually needs before any data is touched. They read as one process — scoping the work — and are always addressed together in stakeholder conversations. Each step builds on the previous one.

clusters.title: Recommendations and Plain-Language Translation
clusters.reasoning: Forming a data-driven recommendation and translating it into plain language are two steps of the same communication act: deciding what to say and then saying it in terms the stakeholder understands. A recommendation that cannot be translated into plain language is not yet complete. They read as two parts of one idea: communicating a finding as an actionable recommendation.

clusters.title: Prioritizing Findings and Framing Recommendations
clusters.reasoning: Prioritizing findings by relevance (selecting which results matter most to the stakeholder) and framing recommendations as actionable (stating what to do, not just what was found) are two aspects of the same editorial decision: what to lead with and how to say it. Narrative context setup is about structuring the opening of a presentation, which is a distinct communication skill.

clusters.title: Tailoring Detail and Anticipating Questions
clusters.reasoning: Tailoring the level of detail to the audience and anticipating their questions and objections are two aspects of audience-aware communication. Both require the analyst to model the stakeholder's perspective: what do they need to know, and what will they push back on? They read as two parts of one idea: preparing a presentation for a specific audience.

clusters.title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
clusters.reasoning: Choosing the right chart type for the point being made and simplifying charts for a non-technical audience are two aspects of the same skill: making a visualization communicate clearly. They read as two parts of one idea: chart design for stakeholder communication.

clusters.title: Structuring Presentations and Writing Executive Summaries
clusters.reasoning: Presentation structure (opening, findings, recommendation, appendix) and executive summary writing (one-page distillation of the key finding and recommendation) are two formats for the same communication goal: delivering analytical results to a stakeholder. They read as two variants of one idea: how to organize and present findings.

clusters.title: Defining the Question and Planning the Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Defining the business question, selecting the data retrieval method, and structuring the end-to-end workflow are three sequential planning steps for a capstone project. They form one idea: scoping and planning an analysis before executing it. A learner cannot choose a retrieval method without a defined question, and cannot structure the workflow without knowing both.

clusters.title: Integrating SQL, Spreadsheets, and pandas
clusters.reasoning: Integrating SQL, spreadsheets, and pandas are three parallel tool-application steps in the capstone workflow — each applies one of the path's core tools to the project dataset. They read as variants of one idea: using each tool for what it does best in a real analysis. Building the data model is a structural design task that precedes or accompanies tool integration and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Applying Statistics and Building the Visualization
clusters.reasoning: Applying descriptive statistics and building the dashboard or visualization set are two sequential steps of the capstone's analysis and presentation phase: compute the summaries, then visualize them. The statistics inform what to show; the visualization makes it communicable. They read as two parts of one idea: turning data into insight.

clusters.title: Narrating and Delivering the Capstone
clusters.reasoning: The narrated stakeholder summary and the documented/presented deliverable are two forms of the same final output: communicating the capstone results. The narration is the verbal presentation; the documentation is the written artifact. They read as two aspects of one idea: delivering the completed analysis to a stakeholder. Independent execution is the process of doing the work, which is a distinct concept.
